title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the exact degree, the second fact, and the comparison that hides

questions.prompt: A warning painted beside an irrigation channel near Bizerte reads: "The plank over this channel is never thick enough to walk on." The town wants the same warning on a metal sign, but written with the adjective THIN. Which line puts the same warning in correct English?

options.text: The plank over this channel is never too thin to walk on.
The plank over this channel is always too thin to walk on.
The plank over this channel is always thin enough to walk on.
The plank over this channel is always too thin so that nobody can walk on it.

questions.explanation: "The plank over this channel is always too thin to walk on." carries the original warning across. Turning a not enough sentence into a too sentence takes three changes at once, and they travel together: the adjective becomes its opposite on the same scale, enough becomes too, and the negative moves out of the sentence, because too ... to already carries it. Never thick enough therefore becomes always too thin. "The plank over this channel is never too thin to walk on." says the plank always bears a walker, the exact reverse of the warning. "The plank over this channel is always thin enough to walk on." is worse still: adjective + enough + to says that nothing stands in the way, so the sign would be inviting people onto the plank. And "The plank over this channel is always too thin so that nobody can walk on it." has the meaning right and the English wrong: too ... to already carries the negative, and so that nobody can marks it a second time.

questions.prompt: Rania wants the first line of her report on the new treatment plant to open on the words "Not only". Her two facts: the plant purifies the town's waste water, and it sells the treated water to three farms. Which opening is correct English?

options.text: Not only the plant purifies the town's waste water, but it also sells the treated water to three farms.
Not only the plant does purify the town's waste water, but it also sells the treated water to three farms.
Not only does the plant purifies the town's waste water, but it also sells the treated water to three farms.
Not only does the plant purify the town's waste water, but it also sells the treated water to three farms.

questions.explanation: "Not only does the plant purify the town's waste water, but it also sells the treated water to three farms." is the correct opening. Here Not only carries what is said about the plant, the verb and everything that follows it, and English then puts the auxiliary in front of the subject exactly as it does in a question; the verb purify has no auxiliary of its own, so does appears and takes the tense, leaving the main verb in the bare form. "Not only the plant purifies the town's waste water, but it also sells the treated water to three farms." keeps the word order of an ordinary statement: that order is the right one when the pair joins two subjects, as in Not only the pipes but also the tank is leaking, but here it joins two things said about one subject, so the auxiliary has to come first. "Not only does the plant purifies the town's waste water, but it also sells the treated water to three farms." brings in does but marks the tense twice, on the auxiliary and on the verb; after does the verb keeps its bare form. And "Not only the plant does purify the town's waste water, but it also sells the treated water to three farms." puts does after the subject instead of before it, which is emphasis, not inversion.

questions.prompt: A leaflet from the water company contains this line: "Farming accounts for about 80 % of the country's water consumption." A pupil has to pass the same information on without using the phrase "accounts for". Which rewrite keeps the meaning?

options.text: Farming uses about 80 % of the country's water.
Farming explains why the country's water consumption is so high.
Farming pays for about 80 % of the country's water.
Farming keeps an account of the country's water consumption.

questions.explanation: "Farming uses about 80 % of the country's water." is the rewrite. To account for a share of a total means to be that share of it, and consumption is the amount used up, so the leaflet is saying that farming is the user of four fifths of the water. "Farming explains why the country's water consumption is so high." takes the other meaning of account for, to give the reason for something; the leaflet gives a proportion, not an explanation, and a share and a cause are not the same claim. "Farming pays for about 80 % of the country's water." reads the word account as money, the trap the noun sets for anybody translating word by word. And "Farming keeps an account of the country's water consumption." turns farming into a bookkeeper: to keep an account of something is to record it, which is what a meter does, not what a farm does.

questions.prompt: A caretaker in Sfax had written this notice: "Not only the meter but also the taps have been changed." He then decides to name the meter second, because it is the more expensive of the two jobs. What must his new notice say?

options.text: Not only the taps but also the meter have been changed.
Not only the taps but also the meter has been changed.
Not only the taps but also the meter had been changed.
Not only the taps but also the meter, they have been changed.

questions.explanation: "Not only the taps but also the meter has been changed." is the new notice. When not only and but also join two subjects, one verb serves them both and it agrees with the NEARER one, the one that follows but also; the caretaker has moved the singular meter into that position, so have has to become has. Nothing is inverted here, either: the pair is holding two subjects together, not opening on what is said about them. "Not only the taps but also the meter have been changed." keeps the plural verb of the first notice and makes it agree with the taps, which now stand furthest from the verb: it is the commonest mistake with this structure. "Not only the taps but also the meter had been changed." changes the tense instead of the agreement: had been changed places the work before some other moment in the past, and the notice is about a job that has just been done. And "Not only the taps but also the meter, they have been changed." adds a pronoun that repeats the subject already there; English builds this structure with one subject group and one verb.

questions.prompt: Emna is writing the last line of her article on the old aqueduct above the valley. She wants to say that the aqueduct carried the life of the town, and she wants a METAPHOR. Which of these four lines is the one she is looking for?

options.text: The aqueduct was like a vein running under the fields.
The aqueduct was as necessary to the town as a vein.
The aqueduct was the vein of the town.
The aqueduct complained under the weight of the water.

questions.explanation: "The aqueduct was the vein of the town." is the metaphor: it states the comparison as a fact, with no like and no as, and leaves the reader to work out in what way an aqueduct is a vein. An aqueduct and a vein are things of two different kinds, so a figure of style is really at work here, and the missing sign is what makes it a metaphor rather than a simile. "The aqueduct was like a vein running under the fields." announces the comparison with like, which is the sign of a simile. "The aqueduct was as necessary to the town as a vein." announces it with the other sign, as ... as, so it is a simile too, and it even names the point of comparison, which is the opposite of saying nothing. And "The aqueduct complained under the weight of the water." gives a human action to a thing, which is a personification, the third name your book offers and a different figure from the one she wants.

questions.prompt: Your grammar summary opens its entry on adverbs of degree with this rule: an adverb of degree modifies an adjective OR another adverb, and stands in front of it. In which of these four lines does the adverb of degree modify another ADVERB?

options.text: The tap in the yard was quite loose.
The lorry was too heavy for the old bridge.
The guide was very friendly.
The volunteers worked extremely carefully.

questions.explanation: "The volunteers worked extremely carefully." is the line: carefully answers the question HOW they worked, so it is an adverb, and extremely stands in front of it to say how much. In "The tap in the yard was quite loose." the word after quite is loose, which tells you what the tap WAS, not how anything was done, so it is an adjective. "The lorry was too heavy for the old bridge." works the same way: heavy describes the lorry itself. And "The guide was very friendly." is the trap of the set: friendly ends in -ly, which usually marks an adverb, but here it follows was and describes the guide, so it is an adjective, exactly like lovely, lonely and daily in the same position.
